output.learning_objective: Convert between probability, odds and log-odds, and explain why log-odds can take any real value while probability cannot.

make.text: Probability lives between 0 and 1, which makes it awkward to model with a straight line. Odds and log-odds re-express the same belief on a scale with no ceiling or floor.

make.request: Walk through p = 0.8 step by step: odds = 0.8/0.2 = 4 (4 to 1 in favour), then log-odds = ln 4, about 1.39. Show p = 0.5 giving odds 1 and log-odds 0. Point out that odds are not the same thing as probability: 0.8 versus 4.

Plot log-odds on the vertical axis against probability from 0 to 1. Mark p = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. Show the curve falling to negative infinity near 0 and rising to positive infinity near 1, so log-odds cover all real numbers.

make.text: Before we check: if p = 0.2, would you expect the odds to be above or below 1, and the log-odds positive or negative?

make.request: Give one short problem on a new case: a team wins with probability 0.25. Have the learner find the odds and the log-odds sign, and say what happens to log-odds as the win probability approaches 1. Do not reuse p = 0.8.

checks.prompt: A team wins a game with probability 0.25. Which statement about its odds and log-odds is correct?

options.label: Odds are 0.25 and log-odds are positive
Odds are 1/3 and log-odds are negative
Odds are 3 and log-odds are positive

checks.prompt: In your own words: why can log-odds be any real number even though a probability must stay between 0 and 1? Use a probability like 0.99 or 0.01 as an example.

output.learning_objective: Explain that a plant's mass is built mostly from CO2 and water using light energy, with soil supplying only minerals, and apply that to a new case.

make.text: A bean seedling can grow into a big plant. Where do you think all that new mass comes from? Hold your guess; we will test it.

make.request: A bean seedling growing in light. Show arrows into the plant: CO2 from air and water from roots feeding sugar-making in the leaves, light as an energy arrow (not matter), and a small side arrow for soil minerals. Label which arrows carry most of the mass.

Using the bean seedling, explain in plain words, with no math, that the plant builds its sugar from CO2 and water, light supplies the energy to do it, and soil supplies only small amounts of minerals. Include the classic idea that a tree grown in a pot loses almost no soil mass while gaining a lot of its own.

Give one short scenario on a new case, not a bean: a sunflower grown in a sealed glass jar of soil with water added, in bright light, with air that can enter. Ask the learner to say where most of the new mass came from and what the soil and light each contributed.

checks.prompt: A young oak tree grows in a big pot for several years, getting only light, air and water. At the end it weighs 30 kg more, while the soil has lost almost no mass. Where did most of the oak's new mass come from?

options.label: Mostly from CO2 in the air and water
Mostly from minerals taken out of the soil
Mostly from the light itself turning into matter
Mostly from the pot absorbing nutrients

checks.prompt: A friend says a cactus in a desert must get its bulk from the sand it grows in. In your own words, explain what you would tell them about where the cactus gets its mass, and what the sand and sunlight do contribute.
